_: Production lines of the director. A line is just config: the engine, its SPEC.md, example films, aspect and sizes, the house tone. A line is available when its SPEC.md exists. Example folders that are missing are found by scanning films/ for index.html files that load the engine (films/studio is never used as an example). Read by films/director/*.py and check.cjs. style_refs are hand-built films named to the coder as a look reference only (their code is not a spec).

battle-map.default_tone: upbeat with a glint of dark humour, kid-clear (ages 8 to 14), like a favourite teacher who loves this story
battle-map.structure: l00 is the hook (a promise or a surprising fact, the year in it). l01 is the title line, exactly "The Battle of X." (or the film title for a non-battle subject). Then the build-up (who, where, why), the plan, the clash, the turn, the result, and a closing line with a smile (a consequence we still feel today, or a dry joke).
battle-map.picture_rules: Every line needs ONE clear picture idea that a child could follow on a map: who is where (two clear colours), what moves (blocks, arrows that draw on), names and numbers that pop in at the word. Losses are numbers and fading blocks, never wounds.
battle-map.end_card: BATTLE MAP over the last outro seconds, with the battle name and year
battle-map.music_prompt: Epic but playful orchestral adventure score for a kids history animation: bold brass, war drums, a driving rhythm with folk colour fitting the period and place, bright and heroic, around 110 BPM, a tense middle section, a triumphant end. Instrumental only, no vocals.
battle-map.voice_brief: an upbeat, warm, playful, completely natural-sounding narrator for an animated history map for kids, with dry deadpan humour
battle-map.voice_instructions: Warm, upbeat, playful storyteller narrating an exciting animated history map for kids aged 8 to 14. Natural and conversational, like a favourite teacher who loves this story: real energy and a smile in the voice, a dry deadpan touch on the jokes, a little awe on the big moments. Never robotic, never a movie-trailer announcer. Brisk pace, natural pauses.
spec_rules: Read the cues: every narrated idea gets its picture AT the word (labels, icons, arrows, moves start on cue words like 'l05.charged'). Copy words exactly from the word lists given; a wrong word is a hard error.
Two clear team colours for the two sides (team 'rome' = deep red, 'carthage' = royal blue; 'gold' or 'green' for a third party), explained by labels the first time each side appears.
A stylised but recognisable map of the real place (coastlines, rivers, hills, roads), map units with x east and z south; keep every block, label and arrow inside the world size.
Use a second stage (stages + a full-screen inset) for the battlefield close-up when the story moves from the region to the field, as in the examples.
Camera: start at t 0, a motivated move per line (push in on the action, top-down for manoeuvres, low obliques for drama), keys in time order, 'spline' for sweeps.

Title card: the film title and the year over the title line (scrim card, as in the examples). End card over the outro (the last cues.outro_s seconds): BATTLE MAP, then the title and year in italic, until the end of the film.

Kid-safe: armies are blocks, arrows and banners; losses are counters and fading blocks, never wounds. On-screen words in CAPITALS, short (at most 4 words), set in code; no em or en dashes and no '...'.
Labels must not cover each other: when two show at once, offset them with dx/dy or give them different times; keep screen-anchored text between 0.06 and 0.94 of the frame.
Keep the spec under about 35 KB; plain data plus small helpers (Object.fromEntries, map) like the examples; no imports, no randomness, no clocks.

No emoji and no clip-art icons (heart, hug, question, star, no, check, burst are rejected); use labels, the legend, banners, arrows and moves. A `legend` (sides, units, key places) frames the battlefield when the engine supports it.

Write `scenes` first as the engine SPEC.md says (5 to 9 scenes, each with its `job`, then its shots with `why`, `from` and motivated `moves`); the checks reject a spec without it and refuse camera moves faster than a real camera.
Every cut has a written `why` (new information, place, time, reaction or scale). Add the `legend` and `ambient` blocks the SPEC.md describes.
battle-map.music_style: ambient, warm and living, like the Age of Empires and Anno soundtracks (Sam, 22 Oct): a calm bed under the narration, not a full score

craft._: CRAFT.md section 9 checks done in code by check.cjs (and lint/battle-map.js for the camera)

kinetic.default_tone: plain, restrained, adult; facts carry the weight, no sensationalism
kinetic.structure: l00 is the hook (a document, a date or a number that stops the scroll). l01 is the title line (the film title). Then the story in beats linked by but and therefore, each beat a word, a date, a number, a document or a quote, and a closing line that lands quietly.
kinetic.picture_rules: Every line needs ONE clear typographic picture idea: the key word, date, number or quote that appears on screen at the word. Real atrocities are shown with restraint: objects, documents, light, absence, symbols. No gore.
kinetic.end_card: the series card over the last outro seconds
kinetic.music_prompt: Dark, restrained, cinematic underscore for a true-history short: low strings, a sparse piano motif, soft pulses, slowly building tension, no big drops, a quiet resolved ending. Instrumental only, no vocals.
kinetic.voice_brief: a calm, grave, completely natural-sounding documentary narrator
kinetic.voice_instructions: Calm, grave, natural documentary narrator. Plain and restrained, no drama in the voice, the facts carry the weight. Measured pace, real pauses.
spec_rules: Read the cues: every narrated idea gets its words, dates, numbers or quotes on screen AT the word. Copy words exactly from the word lists given.
Title card over the title line; the series end card over the outro (the last cues.outro_s seconds).
Restraint: no gore, nothing shown suffering; documents, objects, light and absence carry the story. No em or en dashes and no '...' on screen.
Keep every text inside the 9:16 safe area; no imports, no randomness, no clocks.
Write `scenes` first: 5 to 9 scenes, each `{ name, at, until, begin, middle, end, why }`; the check rejects a spec without it.
